lead: An event B often arrives as the sum of parts. If the sample space is cut into cases A₁, …, Aₙ that do not overlap and together cover everything, then P(B) is the sum of P(B|Aᵢ)P(Aᵢ). That is total probability. Bayes' theorem runs the same arithmetic backwards: from P(B|Aⱼ) it gives P(Aⱼ|B). Spam filters, medical test reports, quality control on a shop floor and UPI fraud scoring all use this reversal.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.2 for conditional probability and the multiplication rule.

sections.h3: A partition turns one event into weighted cases

blocks.text: A partition of the sample space Ω is a list of events A₁, A₂, …, Aₙ with two properties. They are pairwise disjoint: Aᵢ ∩ Aⱼ = ∅ when i ≠ j, so no outcome sits in two cases. They cover the space: A₁ ∪ A₂ ∪ … ∪ Aₙ = Ω, so every outcome sits in some case. Each case also needs P(Aᵢ) > 0, otherwise P(B|Aᵢ) is undefined.
A partition breaks one hard probability into n easy ones. Count B inside each case, then weight by the size of that case.

blocks.where: B is any event; A₁, …, Aₙ is a partition of Ω; P(Aᵢ) is the probability of case i, also called its weight; P(B|Aᵢ) is the conditional probability of B inside case i.

items: Name the cases and check them: disjoint, and union equal to Ω.
Write down each conditional probability P(B|Aᵢ).
Multiply each pair and add the products.
Check that the answer lies between 0 and 1.

blocks.text: Each term P(B|Aᵢ)P(Aᵢ) equals P(B ∩ Aᵢ) by the multiplication rule from Chapter 2.2. The pieces B ∩ A₁, …, B ∩ Aₙ are disjoint and their union is B, so their probabilities add. That is the whole proof. A shop floor gets items from two machines: M1 makes 60% and M2 makes 40%, with defect rates 2% and 5%. The cases are the machines, B is "the item is defective", and the figure shows the arithmetic.
Total probability travels from the cases to B. Bayes' theorem travels back: it turns P(B|Aⱼ) into P(Aⱼ|B).
P(Aⱼ|B) = P(B|Aⱼ) P(Aⱼ) / P(B) = P(B|Aⱼ) P(Aⱼ) / Σᵢ P(B|Aᵢ) P(Aᵢ)
blocks.where: Aⱼ is the case you are asking about; B is the observed event; P(Aⱼ) is the prior; P(B|Aⱼ) is the likelihood; Σᵢ P(B|Aᵢ)P(Aᵢ) is the evidence, the total probability of B.

items: Prior P(Aⱼ): what you believed about case j before seeing B.
Likelihood P(B|Aⱼ): how well case j explains the evidence B.
Evidence P(B): how likely B is under all cases together.
Posterior P(Aⱼ|B): what you believe about case j after seeing B.

blocks.text: The denominator is compulsory. The numerator P(B|Aⱼ)P(Aⱼ) is only the joint probability P(Aⱼ ∩ B). Dividing by P(B) turns it into a conditional probability, and it rescales the n products so that the posteriors over all cases add to 1.
In an exam, write the denominator as the full sum before you put in any numbers. A forgotten case then shows up immediately as a wrong total.

sections.h3: Base rates: why a 99% test can still be wrong

blocks.text: A base rate is the prior P(A) when that prior is small, and a small prior pulls the posterior down hard. A condition affects 1 person in 1000, so P(D) = 0.001. A test is positive for 99% of affected people, P(+|D) = 0.99, and for 5% of unaffected people, P(+|Dᶜ) = 0.05. One person tests positive. What is P(D|+)?

Out of 100000 people, 99 + 4995 = 5094 test positive, and only 99 of those are affected. So P(D|+) = 99/5094 ≈ 0.0194. The formula gives the same number: P(D|+) = (0.99 × 0.001) / (0.99 × 0.001 + 0.05 × 0.999) = 0.00099 / 0.05094 ≈ 0.0194.

A positive result lifts the chance from 0.001 to about 0.019, roughly nineteen times higher, and still under 2%. The likelihood 0.99 was never the answer. A two-way table of counts is the fastest way to see this, and it works on any base-rate question.

figure.caption: Total probability adds the defect contributions from the two machines: 0.012 + 0.020 = 0.032.

spec.title: Defect probability
spec.aria: Block diagram: machine M1 makes 60 percent of items at 2 percent defect and contributes 0.012; M2 makes 40 percent at 5 percent and contributes 0.020; the two contributions add to a total defect probability of 0.032.

examples.question: Machine M1 makes 60% of the items in a lot and machine M2 makes the remaining 40%. The defect rate of M1 is 2% and the defect rate of M2 is 5%. An item is picked at random. (a) Find the probability that it is defective. (b) Given that it is defective, find the probability that it came from M1.
steps: Define the events: A₁ = "item came from M1", A₂ = "item came from M2", D = "item is defective".
Read the weights and likelihoods: P(A₁) = 0.60, P(A₂) = 0.40, P(D|A₁) = 0.02, P(D|A₂) = 0.05.
Check the partition: A₁ and A₂ are disjoint and together cover every item, and both weights are positive.
Joint contributions: P(D ∩ A₁) = 0.60 × 0.02 = 0.012 and P(D ∩ A₂) = 0.40 × 0.05 = 0.020.
Total probability: P(D) = 0.012 + 0.020 = 0.032, that is 3.2% of items are defective.
Check: P(A₂|D) = 0.020 / 0.032 = 0.625, and 0.375 + 0.625 = 1, so the posteriors add correctly.
examples.answer: P(defective) = 0.032 and P(M1 | defective) = 0.375, so 37.5% of the defectives come from M1 even though M1 makes 60% of the output.
examples.check:
p1, p2 = 0.60, 0.40
pd1, pd2 = 0.02, 0.05
c1 = p1 * pd1
c2 = p2 * pd2
pd = c1 + c2
post = c1 / pd
print(round(c1, 4))
print(round(c2, 4))
print(round(pd, 4))
print(round(post, 4))

traps: Dropping P(B) from the denominator. P(A|B) and P(B|A) are different numbers, and the denominator is exactly what turns one into the other.
Swapping the condition. Here P(defective|M1) = 0.02 while P(M1|defective) = 0.375; the two answer different questions.
A partition that overlaps or leaves a gap. If the cases share outcomes or miss part of Ω, the sum for P(B) is wrong even if every multiplication is right.
Using the likelihood alone as the weight. Every term needs P(B|Aᵢ) multiplied by P(Aᵢ); a 0.99 likelihood on a rare case still gives a small joint probability.

quiz.q: State the two conditions an event list A₁, …, Aₙ must satisfy to be a partition of Ω.
quiz.a: Pairwise disjoint, Aᵢ ∩ Aⱼ = ∅ for i ≠ j; and exhaustive, A₁ ∪ A₂ ∪ … ∪ Aₙ = Ω. Also P(Aᵢ) > 0 for every i.

quiz.q: Write the total probability formula for a partition A₁, …, Aₙ and an event B.
Why can you not compute P(A|B) from P(B|A) alone?
quiz.a: P(B|A) says nothing about how common A and B are overall. You also need the prior P(A) and the evidence P(B), which is the total probability over all cases.

quiz.q: Urn 1 holds 2 red and 3 white balls; urn 2 holds 4 red and 1 white ball. An urn is picked by a fair coin and one ball drawn. Find P(red) and P(urn 1 | red).
Three suppliers A₁, A₂, A₃ supply 50%, 30% and 20% of a stock with defect rates 2%, 3% and 5%. Find P(defective) and P(A₂ | defective).

A disease has prevalence 0.001. A test detects every true case and gives a false positive for 1% of healthy people. A patient tests positive. Find P(disease | positive) and explain the size of the answer.
quiz.a: P(D|+) = (1.00 × 0.001)/(1.00 × 0.001 + 0.01 × 0.999) = 0.001/0.01099 ≈ 0.091. Only about 9 in 100 positives are true cases, because the 999 healthy people per 1000 generate about 10 false positives for every one true positive.

beyond: Not for the exam. Apply the same formula once per word, assuming words are independent given the class, and you get the naive Bayes classifier used for spam filtering and text tagging. Replacing the single prior with a whole distribution over parameters leads to Bayesian inference and to Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling. Useful search terms: naive Bayes text classification, Bayesian networks, prior sensitivity.
